data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["In ensemble ML, base classifiers are typically trained to convergence on the same task; non-expert panelists are undertrained and rely on the checklist to substitute for missing expertise.","ML ensembles combine scores algorithmically; human panels may use social aggregation (majority vote, discussion) that introduces conformity bias not present in algorithmic ensembles.","Checklist items in a human panel require subjective perceptual judgment, whereas ML base classifiers produce deterministic outputs for fixed inputs."],"overturn_conditions":["If experts are shown to already subconsciously check the same features the checklist encodes, the checklist adds no new information and the panel is just a noisier version of the expert.","If non-expert panelists are found to be below chance on checklist items that require tacit knowledge, aggregation amplifies error rather than cancelling it."],"shared_structure":["A structured aggregation of weaker classifiers (non-experts + checklist) is compared against a single strong classifier (expert intuition) for a verifiable target.","The weaker classifiers must be individually above-chance and collectively diverse for aggregation to win.","The checklist functions as a shared feature template that constrains the weaker classifiers' decision space."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001","SRC_003","SRC_004"],"transfer_claims":["As in ensembles, the panel's advantage should be largest in the 'medium difficulty' regime where the expert is fallible but non-experts can contribute signal.","As in ensembles, if the checklist (shared feature template) omits a critical feature, all base classifiers are correlated in their blindness and the panel fails together\u2014no amount of aggregation recovers the missing feature."]},"claim":"For objectively verifiable tasks, a trained non-expert panel using an explicit checklist will be more reliable than a single expert using intuition, but only when the checklist encodes the causal features that determine the outcome and the panel's aggregate judgment suppresses individual noise.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the task outcome depends on holistic pattern recognition that trained experts possess but non-experts lack (e.g., radiological diagnosis), a checklist of surface features will be incomplete and the panel will underperform.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's intuition is itself well-calibrated and operates on the same diagnostic features the checklist encodes, the panel's extra noise may exceed its benefit.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If panel members' judgments are not independent\u2014e.g., they discuss before scoring\u2014the error-cancellation mechanism fails and the panel may merely amplify a shared checklist misreading.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Checklists force decomposition of a complex judgment into independently checkable sub-claims. When each item maps to an objectively verifiable sub-condition (e.g., 'Does the specimen show feature X?'), the panel converts an opaque holistic judgment into a structured evidence-accumulation process. Aggregation across non-experts then cancels idiosyncratic perceptual errors (wisdom of crowds), while the checklist cancels systematic omission errors that plague expert intuition. The net reliability gain depends on the checklist's coverage of the outcome-determining feature space.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
